newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada union ready to keep striking if no deal with GM.
newsitem.headline: Canada union ready to keep striking if no deal with GM.

text.p: The president of the Canadian Auto Workers said Friday he was optimistic a deal could be reached to end a 2-week-old strike at General Motors but was also preparing to man the picket lines even longer.

"I've expressed some optimism on the part of our union that we can do this by the (Monday) deadline we've established," CAW President Buzz Hargrove told 600 delegates attending a special dues assessment convention.

He said the $37 million strike fund needed a boost from the union's 210,000 members if its 26,000 striking members at GM Canada remained on the picket lines past Nov. 13 to press the union's demands to limit GM Canada's ability to shift work to outside suppliers, a process known as outsourcing.
"This thing could fall apart," he said. "I'm not at all totally confident this thing will conclude Monday. I'm cautiously optimistic."

At the meeting, delegates from the various locals of Canada's largest private sector union approved a special dues collection to boost the $37 million strike fund to keep paying the striking workers about $92 a week to stay on the picket lines indefinitely.

The plain-spoken union leader said he had letters from around the world offering the union moral and financial support to help him fight one of the world's largest corporations on the thorny issue of contracting out jobs.

He swelled with pride as he told members that major Canadian unions had already offered the CAW over $12 million in interest-free loans and that a tiny nurses' union in California had written to offer its financial support.
"It is incredible the number of messages of solidarity and offers of support that we have got," he said.

He said a stalemate in talks ended on Wednesday after General Motors Chief Executive Jack Smith flew to Toronto to meet with Hargrove and agreed to accept limits on the automaker's outsourcing decisions in order to end a sit-in occupation of a fabrication plant.
Hargrove received thunderous applause from the delegates as he told them of Smith's reaction to the takeover of the Oshawa, Ontario plant about 30 miles (50 km) east of Toronto.
"Mr Smith was taken aback by this issue and he said to me that this is not going to leave a very good impression on the leadership of General Motors," Hargrove said.
He said he told Smith that the union was fed up with the Canadian executives and that he should tell them to get back to the bargaining table.
"Before the two hours was up that's exactly what happened."

GM Canada spokesman Stew Low said that there was a lot of work needed to get an agreeement by Monday, but he was encouraged that the union agreed to recognise that GM was different from Chrysler Corp. and Ford Motor Co.
"I know our team is ready to get down to it and try to find what it takes to get a settlement here and get this thing over with," Low said.

Talks between the two sides have foundered since the strike began around midnight Oct 2. GM had refused to agree to the outsourcing limits laid out in the pattern contract reached by Chrysler and the CAW in September.

Workers took over the Oshawa plant on Wednesday after learning that GM Canada was seeking a court injunction to move some critical machinery in an effort to maintain supply to itself and outside customers in the United States.
If an agreement is ratified, the workers could be back at work at GM plants across Canada by Wednesday.
"We could be going back in Wednesday afternoon," Hargrove said Thursday.
The strike has paralysed GM plants throughout Canada and has also idled 7,478 auto workers in the United States and Mexico, General Motors said Friday.
United Auto Workers officials at GM's Lake Orion, Mich., assembly plant said the facility will idle its second production shift starting on Monday, a move that will affect about 2,000 workers.

The plant builds large sedans, including the Pontiac Bonneville, Buick Park Avenue and Oldsmobile 88, 98 and Aurora. It has run short of transmissions that depend on Canadian-made parts, said a spokesman for UAW Local 5960.
